content: Statins are among the most commonly prescribed medications globally. Atorvastatin, the most frequently used statin, is primarily prescribed for the treatment of hypercholesterolemia and dyslipidemia. By lowering cholesterol levels, which serve as a precursor in the steroidogenesis pathway, atorvastatin may potentially reduce testosterone and other androgen levels. Testosterone and other androgens are critical for numerous biological functions. A reduction in androgen levels caused by atorvastatin could have adverse effects in most scenarios. However, in the context of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where excessive androgen levels are a concern, atorvastatin's ability to lower these levels may be beneficial. The primary objective of this study was to measure the extent to which atorvastatin affects total testosterone levels in both males and females, compared to placebo or no treatment. Secondary objectives included evaluating the effects of atorvastatin on free testosterone, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS), the free androgen index (FAI), and withdrawal due to adverse effects (WDAEs) in both males and females, compared to placebo or no treatment. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hypertension Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and two international trial registries, up to November 9, 2020. Additional searches were performed on the websites of the US Food and Drug Administration, the European Patent Office, and Pfizer. There were no language restrictions, and authors of relevant articles were contacted for further published or unpublished data. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the effects of daily atorvastatin use for at least three weeks, compared to placebo or no treatment, on testosterone levels in males or females. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Continuous outcomes were reported using mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), while dichotomous outcomes (e.g., WDAEs) were reported using risk ratios (RR). A fixed-effect meta-analytic model was used to combine effect estimates, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Six RCTs involving 265 participants were included in the analysis. Of these, two studies included male participants with normal lipid profiles or mild dyslipidemia (N = 140), with a mean age of 68 years. Four studies included female participants with PCOS (N = 125), with a mean age of 32 years. In males, no significant difference in total testosterone levels was observed between atorvastatin and placebo (MD -0.20 nmol/L, 95% CI -0.77 to 0.37). In females with PCOS, atorvastatin was associated with reductions in total testosterone (-0.27 nmol/L, 95% CI -0.50 to -0.04), FAI (-2.59 nmol/L, 95% CI -3.62 to -1.57), androstenedione (-1.37 nmol/L, 95% CI -2.26 to -0.49), and DHEAS (-0.63 μmol/L, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.15). Additionally, atorvastatin increased SHBG concentrations in females by 3.11 nmol/L (95% CI 0.23 to 5.99) compared to placebo. No studies included healthy females (i.e., females with normal testosterone levels) or children under 18 years of age. Notably, none of the studies reported on free testosterone levels. In conclusion, atorvastatin did not significantly affect total testosterone levels in males. However, in females with PCOS, atorvastatin reduced total testosterone, FAI, androstenedione, and DHEAS levels, while increasing SHBG concentrations. The certainty of evidence for these findings ranged from low to very low. Further RCTs are needed to better understand the effects of atorvastatin on testosterone levels.
